newsitem.title: UK: FULL TEXT-UK budget changes to corporate taxation.
newsitem.headline: FULL TEXT-UK budget changes to corporate taxation.

text.p: Following is the full text of a UK Treasury press release on changes to corporate taxation announced in the budget on Wednesday:
COMPANIES AND THEIR SHAREHOLDERS --TAX CHANGES TO PROMOTE INVESTMENT BY COMPANIES
Around half a million companies will benefit from a 2 percent cut in corporation tax rates from 1 April 1997 announced by the Chancellor in his Budget today.

Payment of tax credits will be abolished for pension schemes and UK companies (other than charitable companies) on dividends paid on or after today. Other shareholders will generally not be affected by changes to tax credits until 6 April 1999. In addition:
- individuals, including PEP investors, will have the
opportunity during 1999 to switch into Individual Savings Accounts, which will provide a tax-favoured environment for savings;
- and charities will receive compensation through public expenditure for a further five year transitional period from 1999.

Companies will continue to pay advance corporation tax on dividends at the same rate as now. Shareholders will still be able to set off tax credits against their liability to tax on dividends, but the rate of tax credit will fall to 10 per cent from 6 April 1999.

Individual shareholders liable at the lower or basic rate will continue to have no additional tax to pay on their dividends. And the higher rate of tax on dividends will be reduced to 32.5 per cent from 6 April 1999, so individuals liable at the higher rate on all their dividend income will see no change in their tax bills.

Capital allowances will double for small and medium-sized businesses for expenditure on plant and machinery in the next twelve months. This change applies to both companies and unincorporated businesses.
Details are in a separate Inland Revenue Press Release entitled "Higher Capital Allowances for small and medium-sized companies".

Companies' ability to carry back trading losses against earlier profits will be restricted to one year, as was generally the case until 1991. The period was then extended to three years, at a time of recession. But economic circumstances are now very different.

The lower corporation tax rates and higher capital allowances will encourage investment by companies, by increasing their after tax return from investment, and the abolition of payable tax credits will remove a distortion in the tax system which encourages the distribution of profits as dividends rather than their retention and reinvestment.

1.From the financial year 1997 (the year which began on 1 April 1997), the main rate of corporation tax will be reduced from 33 per cent to 31 per cent, and the small companies' rate (which applies to companies with profits up to 300,000 Pounds)
from 23 per cent to 21 per cent.

2.There will be no change in the upper limit of 1,500,000 Pounds for the small companies' marginal relief. (This relief, which applies to companies with profits between 300,000 Pounds and 1,500,000 Pounds, tapers out the benefit of the small companies' rate.)

3.Until 1991, companies and unincorporated businesses could in general carry back trading losses only against profits of the preceding year. The 1991 extension of the period to three years was for companies only. The change announced today will once more align the position of companies with that of unincorporated businesses. It applies to losses arising on or after today.
4.This change will also apply to losses on loan relationships, financial instruments and foreign exchange transactions.

5.A three year carry back will continue to be available for trading losses arising in the twelve months before a trade comes to an end, and for losses due to the special 100 per cent allowance on the costs of decommissioning North Sea oil and gas installations.
6.A UK company has to account for advance corporation tax on its dividends. Advance corporation tax will continue to be payable, at the same rate as now.

7.There is a special regime for foreign income dividends paid out of foreign income. Any advance corporation tax which cannot be set against the company's corporation tax liabiliy is repaid. With the exception of the arrangements for international holding companies, the rules for payment of foreign income dividends will cease to apply from 6 April 1999.

8.International holding companies can pay dividends out of foreign income without paying advance corporation tax. Provision will be made in the next Finance Bill to ensure they will continue to be able to do so.

9.Changes to the tax rules covering payments representative of dividends (manufactured payments) will be made in the next Finance Bill to reflect the wider changes in the taxation of dividends after 6 April 1999. Since dividends will not carry payable tax credits there will no longer be any need for payers of manufactured dividends on UK equities to account for advance corporation tax when they make such payments.

10.Dividends paid by UK companies carry tax credits. They can be set against a UK resident shareholder's liability to tax on the dividend. The value of the tax credit is currently 20 per cent of the sum of the dividend plus the tax credit. For example, the tax credit on a dividend of 800 Pounds is 200 Pounds (that is, 20 per cent of 800 Pounds plus 200 Pounds).
The tax credit satisfies the tax liability of individuals with income only in the lower or basic rate bands. Higher rate taxpayers can set the tax credit against their tax liabilities.

11.When exempt investors such as pension schemes receive dividends they can claim payment of the tax credit from the Exchequer. In the above example the payment would be 200 Pounds. A dividend of 800 Pounds is thus worth 1,000 Pounds to an exempt investor. In contrast, an 800 Pounds rise in the value of the shares in the company is worth 800 Pounds. This gives exempt investors an incentive to press companies to pay dividends rather than retain and reinvest profits.

12.Foreign income dividends do not carry tax credits. Instead the dividends are treated as if they were amounts on which lower rate tax had been paid. Individuals with income only in the lower or basic rate bands have no further tax to pay and higher-rate taxpayers pay tax on these amounts at the difference between the higher and lower rates of income tax. These rules were extended from 8 October 1996 to share buybacks and certain special dividends.
13.The special rules for foreign income dividends will cease to apply from 6 April 1999.

- pension providers and UK corporate shareholders 14.Where a dividend is paid on or after Budget Day, pension providers and most UK corporate shareholders (including authorised unit trusts and open-ended investment companies) will no longer be entitled to payment of tax credits from the Exchequer. Tax credits will, however, continue to be payable to charitable companies and to some others which are entitled to special exemptions and reliefs.

15.From April 1999, the tax credit regime will change for other shareholders. The rate of tax credits will be halved to 10 per cent, and tax credits will no longer be payable to shareholders with no tax liability.

16.Individual shareholders whose income is within the lower or basic rate ands will be liable to tax at 10 per cent on their dividend income. That means the tax credit will continue to satisfy their tax liability on UK dividends. The higher rate on dividend income will be reduced to 32.5 per cent from 6 April 1999. This will compensate for the reduction in the rate of tax credits to 10 per cent, as the following example shows:

17.From 6 April 1999 dividend income which is currently taxable at the rate applicable to trusts (34 per cent) will instead be taxable at 25 per cent. This will compensate trusts for the reduction in the rate of tax credits to 10 per cent.

18.The shareholders who will not be paid tax credits from 6 April 1999 include: PEP-holders and individuals currently paid tax credits on their dividends (because they are below the tax threshold or have personal allowances to set against their dividend income). These will have the opportunity to switch into a new tax-privileged savings vehicle, the Individual Savings Account (ISA). The Government will be consulting on the details of ISAs in due course: legislation will be introduced in time for ISAs to be available to investors during 1999. See separate Inland Revenue Press Release entitled "A new individual savings account" charities. The Chancellor recognises the special position of charities. They will therefore receive compensation, through public expenditure, for the loss of tax credits. This compensation will take the form of a payment to a charity of a percentage of the dividends it receives, and will be phased out over five years from 6 April 1999. The percentage will be:

(For comparison the present tax credit represents 25 per cent of the dividend.) The compensation means that charities will have nearly seven years in which to adjust to the abolition of payable tax credits.

The tax reliefs for investors in venture capital trusts will be kept under review, as will the scheme itself. See the Inland Revenue Press Release entitled "Venture Capital Trust and Enterprise Investment Schemes: sharpening the focus".

19.By virtue of double taxation agreements between the UK and other countries, some overseas shareholders are able to claim payment of all or part of the tax credits carried by the dividends that they receive from UK companies. The changes do not take away that right, but the decrease to 10 per cent in the value of the tax credit will generally reduce or eliminate the amount payable from 6 April 1999.

20.The Finance Bill will contain a measure to prevent avoidance by shareholders of the abolition of ayment of tax credits by, for example, the transfer of dividends to those who can still benefit from a tax credit. This provision will apply from today. It is not intended to preclude bona fide commercial transactions such as ordinary stock lending and repo arrangements, or the hedging of portfolios as part of efficient portfolio management.
21.In addition, as regards dividends paid on or after today:

companies (other than charitable companies) will not be able to obtain the benefit of tax credits received by certain trusts; and unauthorised unit trusts, other than court common investment funds and those dedicated to investment by charities, will be treated as receiving foreign income dividends.
NOTES FOR EDITORS Impact on Exchequer
1.The effects of the changes on tax receipts are as follows:
Cut in main rate of corporation
2.The full effect of the cut in corporation tax rates will not arise until 1999-2000 because companies pay corporation tax nine months after the end of their accounting periods.

3.It is estimated that small and medium-sized businesses will pay 230 million Pounds less tax in 1998-99 and 170 million Pounds less tax in 1999-2000 as a result of the 12-month doubling of capital allowances. There will be some increase in their tax bills in later years as the balance of unrelieved capital expenditure carried forward will be reduced by the higher allowances. They will gain additional allowances on increases in investment and the cash flow benefit of earlier allowances on all their investment in the 12 months from today.

4.The abolition of foreign income dividends from 6 April 1999 will result in an Exchequer yield of 250 million Pounds a year from 2000-01 onwards. The figures for the impact in 1998-99 and 1999-2000 reflect possible behavioural effects, such as bringing forward into 1998-99 foreign income dividends that would otherwise have been paid in 1999-2000.

5.The Exchequer yield from the changes to tax credits allows for investors continuing to obtain some tax relief through Individual Savings Accounts when they are introduced in 1999. (450 million Pounds in 1999-2000 and 500 million Poundsper annum subsequently.) Allowance has also been made for an increase in dividends paid as foreign income dividends in 1997-98 and 1998-99 and a fall in corporation tax from companies increasing their contributions to pension schemes.

6.Reducing the lower and basic rate tax charge on individuals' dividend income to 10 per cent and cutting the higher rate of tax to 32.5 per cent will have an Exchequer cost of 50 million Pounds per annum from 2000-01. This is primarily because the reduction in the rate of tax credits to 10 per cent from 6 April 1999 means the amount of income (equal to the dividend plus the tax credit) falls, to the benefit those who do not pay higher rate tax on all their dividend income.
- international comparisons of company tax rates
7.The UK's main rate of corporation tax will be lower than that in the USA, Japan and Canada, and in other large EU member states.

8.The UK has generally the lowest rate of corporation tax in the EU for profits up to 300,000 Pounds. Most other countries either have no special rate for smaller companies or, if they do, it is above the rate in the UK or applies with a much lower profits limit.

9.Housing Investment Trusts, which are investment trusts that specialise in investing in residential property, will also benefit from the cut in the small companies' rate as they are liable at this rate on their profits from letting eligible property.

10.A company which pays a dividend has to pay advance corporation tax. The rate at which advance corporation tax is charged is currently 20 per cent of the sum of the dividend and the advance corporation tax on it. So a company pays advance corporation tax of 200 Pounds on a dividend of 800 Pounds. The advance corporation tax liability can be set against the company's corporation tax liability within certain limits, which are unchanged.

11.A company can opt to pay a foreign income dividend. It still has to pay advance corporation tax when the dividend is paid. However, to the extent that the dividend is paid out of foreign income the company is subsequently repaid any advance corporation tax which cannot be set against its corporation tax liability.

12.The special arrangements for international holding companies enable international holding companies, which, very broadly, are UK companies mainly owned by foreign shareholders, to pay foreign income dividends without accounting for advance corporation tax. Similar arrangements will apply to achieve substantially the same effect as now when foreign income dividends generally are abolished from 6 April 1999. The necessary provisions will be included in the next Finance Bill.
13.The changes are not expected to have a significant impact on companies' compliance costs.

14.The loss of tax credit payments will reduce the total income of pension schemes and other pension providers by around 3,500 million Pounds in a full year. This is equivalent to between 5 per cent and 10 per cent of pension schemes' total income. The effect on occupational pension schemes will depend on a number of factors, including how far they are in surplus, the extent to which they hold UK equities and the assessment of their ability to meet future commitments in the light of the Budget changes, share values and dividend levels. Like other shareholders, pension schemes will benefit from the better climate for investment by companies.

15.The payment to overseas shareholders of all or part of the tax credits carried by their UK dividends is governed by the terms of any relevant double taxation agreement. Reducing the rate of the tax credit to 10% from 6 April 1999 will mean that most overseas shareholders will either cease to be able to obtain payment of tax credits or see the amount payable fall to less than 1 per cent of the dividends.
